title: The law in letter and in meaning
source_text: Φέρει δ ὁ Κέλσος καὶ τὸ προειρῆσθαι αὐτοῖς μὴ πειθομένοις τῷ νόμῳ τὰ αὐτὰ πείσεσθαι, ἅπερ ἔδρων τοὺς πολεμίους. καὶ πρὶν ἄν τι παρατιθεὶς τούτοις ὁ Κέλσος χρήσηται οἷς νομίζει ἐναντιώμασι πρὸς τὸν νόμον ἀπὸ τῆς Χριστοῦ διδασκαλίας, λεκτέον περὶ τῶν προειρημένων. φαμὲν τοίνυν ὅτι ὁ νόμος διττός ἐστιν, ὁ μέν τις πρὸς ῥητὸν ὁ δὲ πρὸς διάνοιαν, ὡς καὶ τῶν πρὸ ἡμῶν τινες ἐδίδαξαν. καὶ ὁ μὲν πρὸς τὸ ῥητὸν οὐ τοσοῦτον ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν ὅσον ὑπὸ τοῦ ἔν τινι τῶν προφητῶν λέγοντος θεοῦ εἴρηται εἶναι „δικαιώματα οὐ καλὰ“ καὶ „προστάγματα οὐ καλά“· ὁ δὲ πρὸς διάνοιαν κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν προφήτην ἐκ προσώπου τοῦ θεοῦ λέγεται εἶναι „δικαιώματα καλὰ“ καὶ „προστάγματα καλά“· οὐ γὰρ προφανῶς ἐναντία λέγει ὁ προφήτης ἐν ταὐτῷ. ᾧ ἀκολούθως καὶ ὁ Παῦλος τὸ μὲν „γράμμα“ εἶπεν ἀποκτέννειν, ὅπερ ἴσον ἐστὶ τῷ (πρὸς) τὸ ῥητόν· „τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα“ ζῳοποιεῖν, ὅπερ ἰσοδυναμεῖ τῷ πρὸς διάνοιαν. ἔστι γοῦν παρὰ τῷ Παύλῳ ἀνάλογόν τι εὑρεῖν τοῖς νομισθεῖσιν ἂν ἐναντιώμασι κατὰ τὸν προφήτην. ὡς γὰρ ὅπου μὲν Ἰεζεκιὴλ λέγει· „ἔδωκα αὐτοῖς δικαιώματα οὐ καλὰ καὶ προστάγματα οὐ καλὰ, ἐν οἷς οὐ ζήσονται ἐν αὐτοῖς“ ὅπου δέ· „ἔδωκα αὐτοῖς δικαιώματα καλὰ καὶ προστάγματα καλὰ, ἐν οἷς ζήσονται ἐν αὐτοῖς,“ ἤτοι ἰσοδυναμοῦν γε τούτοις· οὕτω καὶ ὁ Παῦλος, ὅπου μὲν τὸ τοῦ νομικοῦ γράμματος διαβαλεῖν θέλει, φησίν· „εἰ δὲ ἡ διακονία τοῦ θανάτου (ἐν) γράμμασιν ἐντετυπω μένη λίθοις ἐγενήθη ἐν δόξῃ, ὥστε μὴ δύνασθαι ἀτενίσαι τοὺς υἱοὺς Ἰσραὴλ εἰς τὸ πρόσωπον Μωϋσέως διὰ τὴν δόξαν τοῦ προσώπου αὐτοῦ τὴν καταργουμένην, πῶς οὐχὶ μᾶλλον ἡ διακονία τοῦ πνεύματος ἔσται ἐν δόξῃ;“ ὅπου δὲ θαυμάζει τὸν νόμον καὶ ἀποδέχεται, πνευματικὸν αὐτὸν ὀνομάζει λέγων· „οἴδαμεν δὲ ὅτι ὁ νόμος πνευματικός ἐστιν,“ ἀποδέχεται δὲ ἐν τῷ· „ὥστε ὁ μὲν νόμος ἅγιος, καὶ ἡ ἐντολὴ ἁγία καὶ δικαία καὶ ἀγαθή.“
pass_a_gloss: Celsus brings (φέρω) also the having been foretold (προλέγω) to them, not obeying (πείθομαι) the law, that they will suffer (πάσχω) the same things which they did (δράω) to the enemies. And before Celsus, setting something alongside (παρατίθημι) these, uses (χράομαι) the things he thinks (νομίζω) contradictions (ἐναντιώματα) to the law from the teaching (διδασκαλία) of Christ, it must be said about the things said before. We say then that the law is twofold (διττός), the one toward the spoken letter (ῥητόν), the other toward the meaning (διάνοια), as also some of those before us taught. And the one toward the letter is said to be, not so much by us as by God speaking in one of the prophets, 'statutes (δικαιώματα) not good' and 'commands (προστάγματα) not good'; but the one toward meaning is said according to the same prophet from the person (πρόσωπον) of God to be 'good statutes' and 'good commands'; for the prophet does not say plainly contrary things in the same [place]. Consistently with which (ἀκολούθως) Paul too said the letter (γράμμα) kills (ἀποκτείνω), which is equal to the literal; but the spirit (πνεῦμα) makes alive (ζῳοποιέω), which is equivalent (ἰσοδυναμέω) to the toward-meaning. There is at any rate in Paul to find something analogous (ἀνάλογον) to the things that might be thought contradictions according to the prophet. For as where Ezekiel says 'I gave them statutes not good and commands not good, in which they shall not live in them', and where 'I gave them good statutes and good commands, in which they shall live in them', or something equivalent to these; so also Paul, where he wishes to disparage (διαβάλλω) the [thing] of the legal letter, says: 'if the ministry (διακονία) of death, engraved (ἐντυπόω) in letters on stones, came to be in glory (δόξα), so that the sons of Israel could not gaze (ἀτενίζω) into the face of Moses because of the glory of his face, the [glory] being abolished (καταργέω), how will not rather the ministry of the Spirit be in glory?' But where he admires (θαυμάζω) the law and accepts (ἀποδέχομαι) it, he names it spiritual (πνευματικός), saying: 'we know that the law is spiritual', and accepts it in: 'so the law [is] holy (ἅγιος), and the commandment (ἐντολή) holy and just (δίκαιος) and good (ἀγαθός)'.
pass_b_english: Celsus also cites the warning given them beforehand, that if they did not obey the law they would suffer the same things they were doing to their enemies. Before Celsus sets beside these passages, and puts to use, what he thinks are contradictions of the law drawn from the teaching of Christ, we must speak about what has been said so far.

We say, then, that the law is twofold: one law according to the letter, the other according to the meaning, as some of those before us have also taught. The law according to the letter is said to be “statutes not good” and “commandments not good” (Ezekiel 20:25), not so much by us as by God, who speaks in one of the prophets; but the law according to the meaning is said by the same prophet, speaking in the person of God, to be “good statutes” and “good commandments” (Ezekiel 20:11). For the prophet does not openly contradict himself in the same place. In keeping with this, Paul too said that “the letter” kills, which is the same as the law according to the letter, but “the spirit” gives life (2 Corinthians 3:6), which is equivalent to the law according to the meaning.

Indeed, one can find in Paul something that answers to what might be thought contradictions in the prophet. In one place Ezekiel says, “I gave them statutes that were not good and commandments that were not good, by which they shall not live” (Ezekiel 20:25), and in another, “I gave them good statutes and good commandments, by which they shall live” (Ezekiel 20:11), or at any rate words equivalent to these. So too Paul, where he wishes to disparage what belongs to the letter of the law, says: “If the ministry of death, carved in letters on stones, came in glory, so that the children of Israel could not gaze at the face of Moses because of the glory of his face, a glory that was passing away, how much more will the ministry of the Spirit be in glory?” (2 Corinthians 3:7–8). But where he admires and approves the law, he calls it spiritual, saying, “We know that the law is spiritual” (Romans 7:14); and he approves it in the words, “So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12).

choices.choice: Editorial supplements (πρὸς) and (ἐν) in Koetschau followed. δικαιώματα rendered ‘statutes’, προστάγματα ‘commandments’ throughout. Ezekiel 20:25 LXX has προστάγματα οὐ καλὰ καὶ δικαιώματα ἐν οἷς οὐ ζήσονται ἐν αὐτοῖς; Origen’s order and wording are loose. There is no verse in Ezekiel reading exactly ‘good statutes and good commandments’; Origen himself adds ‘or at any rate words equivalent to these’. The nearest is Ezekiel 20:11 (‘I gave them my commandments ... by which a man shall live’; repeated in 20:13 and 20:21), so 20:11 is cited. ‘The letter kills ... the spirit gives life’: ‘spirit’ kept lowercase because Origen equates it with the spiritual meaning of Scripture; in 2 Corinthians 3:8 ‘the ministry of the Spirit’ is capitalised as the Holy Spirit. 2 Corinthians 3:8 text: Origen’s πῶς οὐχὶ μᾶλλον ... ἔσται ἐν δόξῃ follows Paul; πῶς οὐχὶ μᾶλλον rendered with the English idiom ‘how much more’. Ezekiel 20:25 and 20:11 are also cited at the first mention of ‘statutes not good’ and ‘good statutes’, earlier in the chapter. ‘Some of those before us’ is unnamed (possibly earlier Christian or Jewish allegorists such as Philo); not identified. οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰσραήλ rendered ‘the children of Israel’.
'brings up the fact that they were told' -> 'cites the warning given them beforehand' (Origen does not concede a 'fact'); ἔδρων imperfect -> 'were doing'
πρὶν ἄν ... χρήσηται sentence reordered into natural English ('sets beside these passages, and puts to use, what he thinks are contradictions')
added inline citations (Ezekiel 20:25) and (Ezekiel 20:11) at the first mention of 'statutes not good' and 'good statutes'
οὐ γὰρ προφανῶς ἐναντία λέγει: 'is not plainly contradicting himself' (ambiguous) -> 'does not openly contradict himself'
τῷ πρὸς τὸ ῥητόν / τῷ πρὸς διάνοιαν: 'the literal sense ... the meaning' -> 'the law according to the letter ... the law according to the meaning' (article refers to the law)
πῶς οὐχὶ μᾶλλον: 'how will ... not be in greater glory' -> 'how much more will the ministry of the Spirit be in glory'
